antipatterns: database/migrations/2026_11_07_190000_add_customer_id_to_orders_table.php:12-34 — branches on DB::getDriverName() and writes the MySQL DDL as raw strings (ALGORITHM=INSTANT/INPLACE, LOCK=NONE, SET SESSION foreign_key_checks). Laravel 13 already provides ->instant(), ->inplace(), ->lock('none') and Schema::withoutForeignKeyConstraints(). Because of this, the schema is defined twice, and the production (MySQL) path is never run by the sqlite test suite

database/migrations/2026_11_07_190000_add_customer_id_to_orders_table.php:25-34 — the column, both indexes and the FK are in one migration. MySQL DDL is not transactional, so if a later statement fails, re-running the migration fails on the column that already exists
app/Console/Commands/LinkOrdersToCustomers.php:30 — the correlated subquery is a raw DB::raw string, while the whereExists just above it uses the builder. The same match condition is written twice
app/Models/Order.php:11 — makes customer_id mass-assignable, which isn't needed if orders are created through the relation
strengths: Has both indexes the endpoint needs: (customer_id, created_at) for the unfiltered list and (customer_id, status, created_at) for the status filter. The leading customer_id also covers the FK
Turns off FK checks so the constraint is added INPLACE without copying the 20M-row table, and restores them in a finally block. nullOnDelete keeps orders after a GDPR delete
Backfill walks primary-key ranges with whereNull + whereExists, which makes it idempotent and resumable. Query-builder updates leave updated_at alone, and unmatched orders stay untouched
latest('id') as a tie-breaker gives stable pagination, and the index supports it because InnoDB includes the PK in secondary indexes
Tests cover updated_at being preserved, re-runs not overwriting existing links, unmatched orders, the empty table, the FK on delete, and that the indexes exist

app/Console/Commands/LinkOrdersToCustomers.php:29 — the null check on the bounds is folded into the for-loop condition, which is hard to read
tests/Feature/CustomerOrdersTest.php:87-126 — the Artisan command tests live in the endpoint test class instead of their own test file
database/migrations/2026_11_08_000002/000003 — the two indexes are in separate migrations. That makes each step safe to retry, but it is a bit more ceremony than needed
strengths: Uses the Laravel 13 schema API for online DDL, which I checked against vendor and in pretend mode against the MySQL grammar: ->instant() on the column, ->inplace()->lock('none') on the indexes and the FK, and Schema::withoutForeignKeyConstraints() for an INPLACE FK add. The resulting DDL is ALGORITHM=INSTANT / INPLACE, LOCK=NONE
One DDL step per migration, so a failed step can be retried safely on non-transactional MySQL DDL
Indexes fit both forms of the query: (customer_id, created_at) and (customer_id, status, created_at)
FormRequest uses 'sometimes','nullable','string', so ?status= still means no filter (tested) and status[]= returns 422
PlaceOrder creates through $customer->orders()->create(), so customer_id stays out of $fillable

--chunk is validated and returns INVALID. Tests check the 'Linked 1' then 'Linked 0' output on a re-run, that updated_at is preserved, that existing links are kept, that unmatched orders are left alone, and that guests get 401

ConvertEmptyStringsToNull turns ?status= into null, so the request now fails with 422 ('The status field must be a string.'). A probe confirmed this. ORDER BY created_at DESC) can't use it for ordering, so MySQL filesorts all of that customer's orders on a heavily used endpoint
antipatterns: database/migrations/2026_11_08_000000_add_customer_id_to_orders_table.php:12-13 — no explicit ->instant() / ->inplace()->lock('none'), so the DDL relies on MySQL picking an online algorithm by itself. ->after('customer_email') stops the column add from being INSTANT on MySQL before 8.0.29. The column and index also share one migration, so a failed index build can't be re-run cleanly
database/migrations/2026_11_08_000001_add_customer_foreign_key_to_orders_table.php:9-10 — a two-line comment that partly restates what the code does
tests/Feature/CustomerOrdersTest.php:18-23 and tests/Feature/LinkOrdersToCustomersTest.php:15-20 — Http::preventStrayRequests() in setUp is ceremony, because nothing here makes HTTP calls
strengths: The cleanest backfill command: the matchingCustomer() builder is reused for both whereExists and the subquery used as the update value, there is no raw SQL beyond the match expression, and it walks primary-key ranges
Disables FK checks while adding the constraint so it isn't added by a table copy. nullOnDelete keeps orders after a customer is deleted
PlaceOrder goes through the relation, and the FormRequest rejects array input
The most thorough tests: a collection-driven set of messy emails, several batches with an output assertion, re-runs keeping links, updated_at preserved, 404 and 401 paths

v.rationale: All three suites pass on sqlite (impl-1 10 tests, impl-2 12, impl-3 16). There is no MySQL server here, so I checked the MySQL DDL by running the migrations in pretend mode against the MySQL grammar. impl-2 ranks first. It does the zero-downtime schema change with Laravel 13's own APIs (instant(), inplace(), lock('none'), withoutForeignKeyConstraints) and puts each DDL step in its own migration so a failed step can be retried. It has both indexes the endpoint needs, and it keeps the ?status= (empty) behaviour through a nullable FormRequest rule. Its weak spot is a raw-SQL UPDATE in the backfill command. impl-1 is functionally correct and has the same online-DDL and index design. But it writes that DDL by hand behind a driver check, so the schema is defined twice and the production path is never tested, and its backfill mixes builder and raw SQL. impl-3 has the most elegant command and the best tests, but it has two real bugs. Its FormRequest turns ?status= into a 422, which a probe confirmed and which the task explicitly calls out. And with only the (customer_id, status, created_at) index, the unfiltered list query has to filesort. It also relies on MySQL's default algorithms instead of asking for online DDL explicitly, and its ->after() keeps the column add from being INSTANT on MySQL before 8.0.29. One limitation shared by all three: re-running the backfill could attach a GDPR-deleted customer's old orders to a new customer who registers with the same email, since customer_email is kept.
